title: Ben Sira and His Book
lead: Jesus son of Sirach, called Ben Sira, was a Jerusalem teacher of wisdom who wrote his book in Hebrew about 180 BC; his grandson translated it into Greek in Egypt after 132 BC. The book, known as Sirach or Ecclesiasticus, is Scripture in the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, is among the Apocrypha for Protestants, and is outside the Jewish Bible, though the rabbis quoted it.

sections.b: Near the end of his book the author signs his name: "I, Jesus son of Sirach Eleazar, of Jerusalem" (Sirach 50:27). "Son of Sirach" gives the book its Greek name, Sirach, and the man his Hebrew one, Ben Sira. He ran a school, a "house of instruction" (Sirach 51:23), for young men, and his book gathers his teaching on God, wisdom, the law, family, money, speech and friendship. His grandson, who does not give his own name, explains in a Greek prologue that he came to Egypt in the thirty-eighth year of King Euergetes, taken to be Ptolemy VIII (132 BC), found the book there, and translated it for Jews "living as foreigners in other lands" (Sirach 1:0). He warns that Hebrew does not carry the same force in Greek, and where the Hebrew survives his Greek often differs.

For centuries the book was known only in Greek, Latin and Syriac. In 1896 pages of the Hebrew were identified among the manuscripts of the Cairo Genizah, the storeroom of an old synagogue, and these medieval copies give about two-thirds of the book. Older Hebrew came from the Dead Sea: a small fragment from Qumran Cave 2 (2Q18) with parts of Sirach 6:14–31, the poem of Sirach 51 in the great Psalms Scroll from Cave 11, and a scroll from Masada with Sirach 39:27–44:17. Comparing them with the grandson's Greek shows a translator who often changed a word or a picture, as he warned his readers he would.

sections.h: Echoes in the New Testament and beyond
sections.b: The New Testament never names Ben Sira, but some of its sayings are close to his. James's "let every person be ready to listen, slow to talk, slow to anger" (James 1:19) matches Sirach 5:11, and James 5:11 ends with God's pity and mercy as Sirach 2:11 does; Jesus' invitation to take his yoke and find rest (Matthew 11:28–30) follows the pattern of Wisdom's yoke (Sirach 6:24–31; 51:26). Whether these are borrowings or shared Jewish wisdom is debated. The early Christian Didache repeats Sirach 4:31 almost word for word (Didache 4:5). The Babylonian Talmud quotes "the book of Ben Sira" by name (Hagigah 13a, quoting Sirach 3:21–22) and records a debate whether it may be read (Sanhedrin 100b).
